metadata.title: Why No Algorithm Can Be Fair Three Ways at Once
metadata.purpose: Show the fairness impossibility theorem: when two groups have different base rates, satisfying all three common fairness definitions simultaneously is algebraically impossible. props.command: Three definitions of fairness — one algorithm — and math says you can't have all three.

props.title: Why No Algorithm Can Be Fair Three Ways at Once

card.copy:
Why No Algorithm Can Be
Fair Three Ways at Once

beats.narration_text: A hiring algorithm scores applicants and recommends who to interview. The company says it's fair. The regulator says: prove it. Three different lawyers walk in with three different fairness definitions, each one obviously reasonable. The first says scores must mean the same thing in both groups. The second says equally qualified people must get the same false rejection rate. The third says equally unqualified people must get the same false approval rate. The algorithm cannot satisfy all three at once. A theorem proves it. That's the paradox.

beats.narration_text: When two groups have different base rates, can a single decision threshold satisfy all three standard definitions of fairness simultaneously?

lines: Can one threshold satisfy all three fairness

card.copy:
Can one threshold satisfy
all three fairness definitions?

beats.narration_text: The three fairness definitions have names. Calibration: when the model says sixty percent risk, sixty percent of those people — in both groups — should actually be high risk. Equal false negative rate: qualified people in Group A and Group B should get rejected at equal rates. Equal false positive rate: unqualified people in both groups should get accepted at equal rates. Each one is defensible. Each one sounds like basic fairness. The problem only emerges when you try to satisfy all three simultaneously with a single threshold.

beats.narration_text: Suppose Group B has a lower base rate of the positive outcome — say fewer are hired in historical data. If the model is calibrated, a score of sixty means sixty percent hire-rate in both groups — fine. But because Group B's overall rate is lower, their score distribution sits to the left of Group A's. A single threshold cuts across both distributions. Move it left to equalize false rejections for Group B — now more unqualified Group B applicants get through, breaking equal false positive rate. Move it back — qualified Group B applicants get rejected at a higher rate. The threshold is one lever and it's pulling three ropes in three directions.

beats.narration_text: Different base rates mean different score distributions — and a single threshold cannot cut two different distributions at the same relative position.
beats.image_description: Two overlapping bell curves — a wide teal one on the right, a narrower crimson one shifted left — with a single vertical gold line cutting through both, the teal area to the right of the cut obviously larger than the crimson area, illustrating the asymmetric cut, dramatic white background with stark geometric clarity

beats.narration_text: Watch the two score distributions — teal for Group A, crimson for Group B, Group B's curve sitting left. The gold vertical threshold sits in the middle. The dials show three live metrics: calibration in green, false negative rate gap in orange, false positive rate gap in orange. Slide the threshold right — the false negative rate gap for Group B spikes. Slide it left — the false positive rate gap spikes. There is no position where all three dials are simultaneously green. The math does not bend.

beats.narration_text: This is a theorem, not a design flaw. Mathematician Alexandra Chouldechova proved in 2017 that when two groups have different base rates, satisfying calibration plus equal false positive rate plus equal false negative rate is algebraically impossible — except in the trivial case where the model is perfectly accurate on both groups. In the real world, no model is perfect. So you must choose which definition to violate. That is a values decision, not a technical one.

beats.narration_text: For AI practitioners, this means fairness is not a checkbox. When a vendor says their model is fair, the first question is: fair by which definition? Because the choice of definition encodes a values judgment about who bears the cost of errors. Equalizing false negative rates means more false positives for some group. Equalizing false positive rates means more false negatives for another. There is no free fairness. Someone pays.

beats.narration_text: The decision about which definition to optimize is a policy decision that should be made explicitly — by humans with accountability — before the model is trained. Instead it is usually made implicitly: whoever writes the loss function chooses without naming the choice. The theorem forces that choice into the open. That is actually useful. A theorem that proves impossibility is a tool for honest conversation.

beats.narration_text: The fix is not a better algorithm — it's a prior conversation. Ask: which group faces the higher cost from false positives? Which group faces the higher cost from false negatives? Who has the power to appeal an error? That conversation determines which fairness criterion should be prioritized. Then build the model to that specification and document which tradeoff was deliberately accepted.

beats.narration_text: A pretrial risk assessment tool predicts whether a defendant will fail to appear in court. Group A has a higher historical failure-to-appear rate in the training data. Group B has a lower rate. The model is calibrated — scores mean the same thing in both groups. But because the base rates differ, a single threshold produces more false high-risk flags for Group B defendants — people who would have appeared, flagged as likely to flee. To equalize that false positive rate, the threshold must move — and now more Group A defendants who genuinely are high-risk get released with low-risk scores. The tool cannot be simultaneously fair by both standards. The jurisdiction must choose — and that choice is a question about who bears the cost of errors in the criminal justice system.

beats.narration_text: When two groups have different base rates, a single decision threshold cannot simultaneously satisfy calibration, equal false negative rate, and equal false positive rate — this is a mathematical theorem, not a fixable engineering problem. For anyone building or auditing AI systems, the implication is that 'fair' is not a property a model has — it's a choice about which error costs which group bears, and that choice must be made explicitly before the model is built.
